rationale: Start with a broad screening gradient spanning the full useful solvent range at mid temperature to reveal the mixture’s overall retention spread and whether any compounds are missing by 42 min. A moderate 20 min gradient balances coverage and resolution for the first information-rich run.

All 10 compounds eluted with excellent resolution, so the clear opportunity is to reduce analysis time while preserving the minimum resolution. A substantially steeper full-range gradient should test how far runtime can be shortened before the closely spaced mid-cluster begins to compress too much.

The 8 min gradient was fast but over-compressed the central cluster, especially peaks 5–7. A small increase in gradient time should selectively recover resolution in that region while keeping total time short and potentially improving CRF over both prior runs.

The 10 min method improved CRF markedly, but the same central pair remains under-resolved, so the optimum likely sits at a slightly longer gradient. Testing 12 min is a focused local refinement to see if resolution crosses the next threshold while still keeping the run in the no-time-penalty region.

Resolution of the critical 6/7 pair is improving steadily as tG increases, and there is still no time penalty at 12 min. A 14 min gradient is the next efficient step to test whether that pair reaches baseline-like separation while maintaining a high overall score.

The limiting pair continues to improve monotonically with gradient time, and 14 min is already very close to ideal. A 16 min gradient should determine whether the critical pair crosses the key resolution threshold and potentially reaches the maximum CRF.

At 16 min the resolution term is maxed out but time penalty lowers CRF, so the optimum likely lies near 14–16 min or could be reached by changing selectivity instead of extending time. Lowering temperature at the faster 14 min gradient may selectively increase retention differences for the critical 6/7 pair enough to hit full resolution without incurring the time penalty seen at 16 min.

Lower temperature worsened selectivity by shifting the bottleneck from 6/7 to 5/6, so the next efficient test is the opposite direction. A modest increase to 45 C at the high-performing 14 min gradient may improve the central selectivity enough to reach full resolution while retaining the zero time penalty.

Temperature changes hurt selectivity, so keep 40 C and instead test a small increase in starting organic to reshape the early-to-mid gradient segment where peaks 5–7 cluster. This may decompress that central group without lengthening the run enough to incur the time penalty seen at 16 min.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved both runtime and the critical 6/7 resolution, suggesting the optimum may lie slightly higher. Testing phi0 0.15 keeps the same successful gradient shape while probing whether the central cluster can be further redistributed without sacrificing the still-safe early separations.

Phi0 = 0.10 gave the best score so far, so now test whether a slightly lower phi1 can flatten the late part of the gradient and improve selectivity within the central cluster. This keeps run time short while probing a more targeted change in gradient steepness than altering tG alone.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 further improved the critical 6/7 pair and raised CRF close to the maximum, so the trend suggests another small decrease may finish the job. Testing phi1 = 0.85 keeps the successful overall method while probing for full resolution without introducing a time penalty.

The maximum score is already reached, so this is only a robustness check near the optimum. Lowering phi1 one more step tests whether the score plateau extends while maintaining full resolution and acceptable run time.

Since lowering phi1 below 0.85 only added time penalty, test whether raising phi0 from the optimal 0.10 to 0.15 can recover some runtime while preserving the full resolution plateau. This is a targeted robustness/plateau check adjacent to the current optimum.

You now have a confirmed CRF plateau at 1.000, so the best use of another injection is to map its boundary toward faster conditions. Increasing phi0 one more step may shorten the run further while testing whether full resolution is still maintained.

Since increasing phi0 to 0.20 left the full-resolution plateau, the next efficient boundary check is a shorter gradient from the successful phi0/phi1 combination. This tests whether tG can be reduced while still keeping the critical 6/7 pair at or above the threshold for CRF 1.000.

The tG and phi0 boundary checks show the optimum plateau is narrow in those directions, so a final local robustness probe is temperature from the best composition/gradient point. Testing 45 C determines whether a small thermal change preserves the 1.000 plateau or sharply degrades the critical central selectivity.

Two methods already achieve the maximum CRF, so further work should only map the neighboring plateau. Combining the successful higher phi0 with phi1 = 0.90 tests whether the 1.000 region extends diagonally in composition space while keeping temperature and tG at the proven optimum.

With the maximum CRF already secured, use remaining injections to learn whether different selectivity settings can also reach the full-resolution plateau. This condition combines a stronger time axis with lower temperature to see if an alternative region exists where the critical mid-cluster is fully resolved.

The best methods indicate a 1.000 plateau near phi1 = 0.85 and tG = 14 at 40 C, bounded on the high-phi0 side by loss of resolution at 0.20. Testing phi0 = 0.05 maps the low-phi0 edge of that plateau and completes the local composition picture around the optimum.

The low-phi0 side at phi1 = 0.85 showed full resolution but incurred a small time penalty, so the remaining unknown near the optimum is whether a slightly higher phi1 removes that penalty while retaining adequate separation. This completes the low-phi0 corner of the local optimum map.

One optimum corner is already known at phi0 0.15/phi1 0.85, and dropping phi1 to 0.80 at phi0 0.10 only introduced time penalty while preserving full resolution. Testing phi0 0.15 with phi1 0.80 checks whether that adjacent point also remains on the 1.000-resolution plateau and helps define its lower-phi1 boundary.

This completes the local 3×4 composition map around the optimum by filling the remaining low-phi0/low-phi1 corner. It will show whether that corner also stays on the full-resolution plateau and define the tradeoff with the onset of time penalty.

The mapped optimum region suggests the practical upper phi0 boundary depends on phi1, with 0.20/0.85 just below full score. Testing 0.20/0.90 checks whether a slightly higher phi1 restores the critical resolution while preserving the faster retention of the high-phi0 corner.

This final run completes the remaining high-phi0/low-phi1 corner around the mapped optimum region. It is the last untested adjacent composition and will fully define the local plateau boundary even though the maximum CRF has already been achieved.
